articles.title: Scientists find a way to fight Alzheimer’s brain damage without removing toxic tau
articles.summary: Scientists have found a promising way to protect the brain from Alzheimer’s-related damage by blocking immune cells that contribute to the destruction of neurons. In mice, the treatment preserved roughly 40% more tissue in memory centers and improved memory, even without removing harmful tau protein buildup.
articles.content:
Protecting brain cells from destruction remains one of the biggest challenges in treating Alzheimer's disease and related neurodegenerative conditions. These disorders, known as tauopathies, involve the buildup of abnormal tangles of a protein called tau inside the brain. As the tangles accumulate, nearby neurons begin to die. However, growing evidence suggests that tau itself may not be responsible for most of the damage. Instead, the immune system's reaction to the protein appears to play a major role in the loss of brain cells, memory, and independence.

Scientists at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis have now identified a promising strategy for interrupting this damaging immune response. In mice with tau accumulation similar to that seen in Alzheimer's, researchers used an antibody to block a protein called CXCR3, which helps immune cells known as T cells enter the brain. After several months of treatment, the number of T cells inside the brain had fallen by approximately half.

The results were striking. Compared with untreated mice, animals receiving the antibody retained roughly 40% more tissue in brain regions involved in memory and performed better on a memory test. These improvements occurred even though the amount of accumulated tau remained unchanged.

The findings were published September 28 in the journal Neuron.

"In tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease, there's no treatment right now that actually decreases neurodegeneration," said David M. Holtzman, MD, senior author of the study and the Barbara Burton and Reuben M. Morriss III Distinguished Professor in the Department of Neurology at WashU Medicine. "If we can show that we're really decreasing brain cell death, it's certainly worth trying to pursue that pathway to prevent the most devastating consequences of these diseases."

Why Immune Cells May Be a Key to Alzheimer's Brain Damage

Current Alzheimer's treatments primarily focus on removing amyloid, another protein associated with the disease. Two approved medications, lecanemab and donanemab, target amyloid plaques that develop between brain cells during the early stages of Alzheimer's. These deposits interfere with communication between neurons, contribute to the formation of tau tangles inside cells, and ultimately lead to neuronal death.

Although these medications can slow cognitive decline, they have not been shown to prevent brain cells from dying. They also offer no treatment for primary tauopathies, conditions in which tau accumulates without the presence of amyloid. Alzheimer's is classified as a secondary tauopathy because both abnormal amyloid and tau are present.

Holtzman's laboratory has been investigating whether the immune system offers another way to address these diseases. In a 2023 study published in Nature, the researchers discovered that T cells enter the brains of mice with abnormal tau accumulation, concentrating in regions containing the most tau and contributing to neurodegeneration.

A related study published earlier this month in Nature Neuroscience provided another important clue. It showed that the signals directing these T cells originate in lymph nodes located outside the brain.

"For this therapeutic approach, if it is safe, you wouldn't have to design the drug to get into the brain -- which is a big deal since most molecules don't cross the blood-brain barrier well -- and you don't have to get rid of the tau to get this therapeutic effect." David Holtzman, MD, WashU Medicine

Scientists Identify the Pathway That Guides Immune Cells Into the Brain

Despite these earlier discoveries, researchers still needed to understand how activated T cells found their way into the brain.

T cells navigate through the body by following chemical signals known as chemokines. Earlier experiments in Holtzman's laboratory had identified unusually high levels of one such signal, CXCL10, in mice with tau accumulation. Other researchers had also reported elevated CXCL10 levels in people with Alzheimer's disease.

Activated T cells carry a surface receptor called CXCR3 that recognizes CXCL10, allowing the cells to follow its chemical signals. This relationship suggested that the CXCL10 and CXCR3 pathway might be responsible for guiding harmful T cells into the brain.

To investigate, the researchers studied mice that developed abnormal tau deposits resembling those associated with Alzheimer's. The team included co-senior author Jason Ulrich, PhD, a professor of neurology at WashU Medicine, and first author Joshua T. Emmerson, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher in Holtzman's laboratory.

The experiments revealed that T cells could not infiltrate the brain when mice lacked either CXCL10 or its matching receptor, CXCR3, on T cells. This protection persisted even when the scientists deliberately triggered inflammation to stimulate an immune response.

Experimental Treatment Preserves Brain Tissue and Memory

With the pathway identified, the team tested whether blocking CXCR3 with an antibody could reduce brain damage.

The researchers selected young mice that already had tau deposits in their brains but had not yet experienced substantial loss of brain cells. They administered the antibody once every five days for three and a half months.

By the end of the experiment, treated mice had approximately half as many T cells in their brains as untreated animals. They also showed less evidence of neuronal injury and retained substantially more brain tissue, including roughly 40% more tissue in memory-related regions. Their performance on a memory test was also better.

Importantly, these protective effects occurred without any detectable reduction in tau tangles. The treated and untreated mice had similar amounts of abnormal tau, suggesting that limiting the immune response could reduce neurodegeneration even when the underlying protein deposits remain.

Another finding could have major implications for future drug development. The antibody reached the boundary of the brain but did not enter the brain tissue itself.

This suggests that it may be possible to reduce neurodegeneration by targeting immune activity from outside the brain. Such an approach could avoid one of the major difficulties in developing neurological treatments: getting drugs across the blood-brain barrier, which prevents many substances from entering brain tissue.

A Potential New Direction for Alzheimer's Treatment

Although the results are encouraging, the treatment has so far been tested only in mice. Additional research will be needed to determine whether the approach is safe and effective enough to evaluate in people.

Holtzman suggested that medications already used to control T cells in other diseases could provide a starting point. Certain treatments for multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune conditions, in which the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy tissue, might be worth investigating for their potential to reduce Alzheimer's-related brain damage.

This would represent a significant shift in treatment strategy. Rather than concentrating exclusively on the abnormal proteins associated with neurodegeneration, researchers could also target the immune responses that contribute to the destruction of neurons.

"Tauopathies aren't thought of as autoimmune disorders, so they haven't been treated the same way, but this study shows for the first time in an animal model that these diseases respond to a specific T-cell therapy," said Holtzman, who also directs WashU's Hope Center for Neurological Disorders and the Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center at WashU Medicine.

"For this therapeutic approach, if it is safe, you wouldn't have to design the drug to get into the brain -- which is a big deal since most molecules don't cross the blood-brain barrier well -- and you don't have to get rid of the tau to get this therapeutic effect."

The findings raise the possibility that protecting the brain from harmful immune activity, rather than removing tau itself, could become an important strategy for treating Alzheimer's and other tauopathies.

The research received support from a BrightFocus Postdoctoral Fellowship, National Institutes of Health/National Institute on Aging grants R01AG082328 and R01AG085374, the GHR Foundation, the Carol and Gene Ludwig Initiative in Neuroimmunology Research, a gift from Ronald Schaich, a gift from John Ludwig, a gift from Cindy and Evan Goldberg, and the Freedom Together Foundation. The study's content is the responsibility of its authors and does not necessarily reflect the official views of the NIH.

Disclosures: DMH co-founded C2N Diagnostics and serves on its scientific advisory board. DMH also serves on the scientific advisory boards of Denali, Genentech, and Switch; provides consulting services to Pfizer, Roche, Novartis, Annexon, and Acta; and serves on the advisory boards of Neuron and Cell.

The article provides detailed context on the mechanism, experimental results, and potential future impact, fulfilling criteria for inspiring good news.

articles.title: Scientists discover a way to kill dangerous gut bacteria without killing the good
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a natural compound that targets dangerous C. difficile bacteria without wiping out the gut's beneficial microbes. Successful early tests suggest it could lead to a gentler, more effective treatment for stubborn intestinal infections that frequently return.
articles.content:
A dangerous intestinal infection may soon have a more targeted treatment option. Scientists have identified a natural compound that can kill the bacteria responsible for severe gut infections while leaving much of the beneficial gut microbiome unharmed.

The bacterium Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) is naturally found in the intestines of many people and generally causes no problems when present in small amounts. However, antibiotics that target a wide range of bacteria can upset the delicate balance of microorganisms in the gut. This disruption allows C. difficile to multiply rapidly, potentially causing severe intestinal inflammation that can become chronic.

C. difficile infections (CDI) are among the leading causes of diarrhea associated with antibiotic treatment. The bacteria produce toxins that can trigger dangerous and sometimes life-threatening inflammation in the intestines. Because these infections frequently return after treatment, scientists are searching for more effective ways to eliminate the pathogen without causing additional damage to the gut microbiome.

A team led by Prof. Rolf Müller, department head and scientific director at HIPS, has now identified a promising drug candidate that specifically targets C. difficile while preserving much of the gut's beneficial microbial community. HIPS is a site of the Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research (HZI) that operates in collaboration with Saarland University.

Natural Compound Targets Dangerous Gut Bacteria

The researchers found that argyrin B, a naturally occurring antibacterial substance, was highly effective against C. difficile in laboratory tests and experiments involving infected mice. Importantly, the compound showed little activity against the beneficial microorganisms that help maintain a healthy digestive system.

"We were able to show that the natural compound argyrin B is highly effective against CDI: both in laboratory experiments and in a mouse model of the infection, where it significantly reduces the bacterial load," says Dr. Jennifer Herrmann, senior scientist in the department "Microbial Natural Products" at HIPS. "An antibacterial target of the argyrins had previously been identified and characterized in the notorious hospital-acquired pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Now we have been able to show that argyrin B also acts on this target in C. difficile and exhibits particularly high efficacy in doing so. In contrast, the argyrins have virtually no effect on the beneficial microorganisms in our digestive tract. The gut microbiome could therefore be spared during treatment with argyrin and restored to a healthy state more quickly."

A Bacteria-Killing Substance Found in Soil

Argyrins were originally discovered in myxobacteria, microorganisms that inhabit soil. These bacteria produce natural substances that help them attack other microbes and use them as a source of food.

Although argyrin B has demonstrated promising antibacterial activity, researchers must also determine whether its pharmaceutical properties make it suitable for use as a medicine. That includes understanding how the compound behaves inside the body and whether it could cause unwanted effects.

One particularly encouraging finding emerged when the team examined what happens after mice receive argyrin B orally. Very little of the compound entered their bloodstream. Instead, most of it remained in the large intestine, where C. difficile infections occur.

By concentrating in the gut rather than circulating throughout the body, argyrin B could potentially reduce the risk of side effects affecting other organs. Together with its selective activity against C. difficile, this characteristic makes the compound a promising candidate for a treatment that may be better tolerated.

Could It Help Prevent Recurring Gut Infections?

One of the biggest challenges in treating C. difficile is its tendency to return. Patients who experience multiple relapses are often treated using fecal microbiota transfer (commonly known as a stool transplant). This procedure aims to restore a healthier balance of gut microorganisms, but it can be complicated to perform and unpleasant for patients.

A medication developed from argyrin could eventually provide another treatment option. By eliminating the harmful bacteria without extensively disrupting the rest of the microbiome, such a therapy might reduce the likelihood of further infections and relapses. That could also help some patients avoid the need for stool transplants.

More research is needed before argyrin B can be considered for clinical use. The scientists plan to investigate which dosage produces the strongest antibacterial effect and use additional experimental models to determine whether the compound can also combat recurring C. difficile infections.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery of a natural compound that selectively kills dangerous C. difficile bacteria while preserving beneficial gut microbes, potentially leading to more effective and gentler treatments for a common and serious intestinal infection with frequent relapses. The research has broad public health implications and is detailed with promising experimental results and future research plans.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between vitamin C and cancer survival
articles.summary: A surprising clinical trial suggests that taking vitamin C daily could improve survival in people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers. Patients receiving the supplement had fewer adverse events and showed a promising survival advantage, raising hopes that a common vitamin could help protect against leukemia-related complications.
articles.content:
Vitamin C plays an important role in keeping the immune system healthy, helping wounds heal, and protecting cells from damage. However, people with precancerous blood disorders and blood cancers often have persistently low vitamin C levels. Researchers have been investigating whether correcting this deficiency could improve their health and treatment outcomes.

New findings from the phase 2 EVITA clinical trial suggest that vitamin C supplementation may offer important benefits for people with precancerous blood conditions and early-stage blood cancers. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study was conducted by the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer® Epigenetics Dream Team.

The results, published in the American Cancer Society journal CANCER, revealed that patients who received 1,000 mg of oral vitamin C every day for one year experienced fewer adverse events during the study and its follow-up period. The supplement also changed the levels of certain immune signaling molecules, known as cytokines, in ways associated with more favorable outcomes. These changes suggest that vitamin C could influence inflammation-related processes involved in the growth and progression of abnormal blood cells.

Although vitamin C did not significantly affect the rate at which abnormal blood cells expanded, the researchers identified an encouraging result. An exploratory analysis showed that participants who received vitamin C were significantly more likely to be alive after approximately three years of follow-up than those who took a placebo. Scientists emphasize that this potential survival benefit must be verified in a larger phase 3 clinical trial.

Vitamin C Shows Promise for Patients at Risk of Leukemia

"We are tremendously excited and cautiously optimistic that our results could one day translate into a simple way to improve care and outcomes for people with pre-leukemia disorders," said Peter A. Jones, Ph.D., D.Sc. (hon), a distinguished professor at Van Andel Institute. Jones is also a co-corresponding author of the research and co-leader of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team.

"Our approach reflects a growing emphasis on cancer interception -- intervening before cancer becomes established. We are working to build on the trial findings by exploring how exactly vitamin C interacts with pre-cancerous cells, including the idea that it may help restore normal epigenetic function in blood cells at risk of becoming leukemia."

The international research effort was led by Kirsten Grønbæk, M.D., Ph.D., a leading hematologist, professor at the University of Copenhagen, and member of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team.

"These exciting preliminary findings lay the groundwork for a larger clinical trial to explore vitamin C as a possible way to improve patient outcomes," said Grønbæk. "It is too early to make definitive recommendations based on our results, but we are hopeful that a more expansive study will provide further insights."

First Clinical Trial Tests Daily Vitamin C for Precancerous Blood Disorders

The study enrolled 109 patients with either clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance (CCUS) or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). Both conditions can develop into acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive form of blood cancer that is often difficult to treat. The likelihood of developing CCUS and related blood disorders rises with age, making these conditions particularly common among older adults.

Currently, no approved treatment can prevent CCUS from progressing to leukemia. Although stem cell transplantation is an option for treating MDS, many patients cannot undergo the procedure because of age or other medical conditions. None of the people enrolled in the trial were receiving cancer treatment when the study took place.

To determine whether vitamin C might offer benefits, researchers randomly divided participants into two groups. One received 1,000 mg of vitamin C by mouth each day for 12 months. The other received a placebo designed to be indistinguishable from the supplement in appearance, taste, and smell, but containing no vitamin C.

Neither the participants nor the clinical staff knew who was receiving vitamin C until the study concluded. This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled approach is considered the gold standard in clinical research because it reduces potential bias and allows investigators to assess treatment effects more objectively.

The research was carried out at four hospitals: Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen University Hospital-Herlev, Aalborg University Hospital, and Keck Hospital of the University of Southern California.

What makes EVITA particularly notable is that it was the first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to investigate oral vitamin C in patients with conditions that can precede leukemia or with lower-risk myeloid cancers. Earlier studies had primarily examined vitamin C administered intravenously and had focused on solid tumors rather than precancerous blood disorders or early-stage blood malignancies.

EVITA instead evaluated a daily oral dose comparable to that available in many over-the-counter vitamin C supplements.

More Than Half of Patients Had Low Vitamin C Levels

Blood samples collected throughout the study allowed researchers to track participants' vitamin C concentrations and determine whether supplementation corrected deficiencies.

At the beginning of the trial, more than half of the participants had insufficient vitamin C levels. Among those assigned to the supplementation group, blood concentrations returned to normal after they began taking vitamin C.

For patients living with conditions that could eventually develop into leukemia, the possibility of an accessible intervention is especially important. In many cases, physicians have little choice but to monitor the disease and watch for signs that it is progressing.

"The standard approach for patients with pre-cancer blood disorders is to monitor their blood cell counts over time. This is, understandably, very frustrating -- no one wants to hear that they have a condition that increases leukemia risk but there's nothing that can be done other than watch and wait," said Casey O'Connell, M.D., FACP, the Lawrence and Jane Kelly Chair in Hematology at the University of Southern California and lead clinician at USC's trial location.

"The EVITA trial took on this challenge by exploring vitamin C's potential to address the underlying factors that drive leukemia development."

How Vitamin C Could Influence Cancer Development

Scientists have investigated whether vitamin C could play a useful role in cancer treatment for more than seven decades. For much of that time, the evidence remained uncertain because studies produced inconsistent findings and employed different experimental methods.

During the past decade, however, improved research technologies have revealed that vitamin C has important functions beyond its familiar roles in nutrition and immunity. In particular, scientists have uncovered its involvement in controlling gene activity and guiding normal cell development.

One of the most important discoveries concerns TET2, an enzyme that helps prevent cancerous growth by controlling whether particular genes are switched "on" or "off." Vitamin C supports the activity of this enzyme, which helps maintain normal patterns of gene regulation.

Mutations affecting TET2 are frequently found in leukemia and related blood disorders. When the enzyme's normal function is disrupted, abnormal cells can gain an opportunity to multiply and potentially develop into cancer.

Experiments using cancer models have provided additional evidence of vitamin C's possible protective effects. These studies found that supplementation could interfere with cellular changes associated with cancer and slow the progression of leukemia. Notably, the strongest effects appeared when vitamin C was introduced before cancer had become established.

This research helped inspire the idea of using vitamin C as a form of early intervention, potentially targeting the biological changes that precede the development of leukemia.

Building Toward Larger Clinical Trials

Before launching EVITA, the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team conducted a pilot clinical study in 2016 to determine whether taking vitamin C orally could meaningfully raise its concentration in the blood.

The initial findings suggested that oral supplementation was a practical approach. Encouraged by those results, the researchers launched the phase 2 EVITA trial in 2017.

"This early work was critical because it offered a foundation from which to develop the present trial," said Stine Ulrik Mikkelsen, M.D., Ph.D., the study's first author and a clinician researcher in Grønbæk's laboratory.

"Vitamin C is important because it is involved in a range of biological functions, including the activity of enzymes that regulate normal cell function."

Researchers are continuing to examine the EVITA data to better understand the biological processes that might explain why patients receiving vitamin C showed improved survival.

Although the findings offer a promising direction for future research, additional clinical studies will be essential to determine whether vitamin C supplementation can reliably improve outcomes for people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers.

Other authors include Ali Al-Mousawi, M.D., Amalie Bach Puglisi, M.D., Anders Pommer Vallentin, M.D., Astrid Østergaard Mortensen, Heidi Naomi Ottesen, Linn Gillberg, M.Sc., Ph.D., Morten Tulstrup, M.D., M.Sc., Ph.D., Jakob Werner Hansen, M.D., Ph.D., and Mette Klarskov Andersen, M.D., D.MSc., of the University of Copenhagen and Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet; Zachary Madaj, M.S., Toshinori Hinoue, Ph.D., Stacey L. Thomas, Ph.D., Christine N. Isaguirre, Ryan D. Sheldon, Ph.D., Marie Adams, M.S., Ryan Burgos, and Peter W. Laird, Ph.D., of Van Andel Institute; Jakob Schmidt Jespersen, M.Sc., Ph.D., Niels Richard Hansen, M.Sc., and Jens Lykkesfeldt, Ph.D., D.MSc., of the University of Copenhagen; Stephen Baylin, M.D., of Johns Hopkins University and Van Andel Institute; Bo Kok Mortensen, M.D., Ph.D., of Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet and Copenhagen University Hospital-Herlev; and Marianne Tang Severinsen, M.D., Ph.D., of Aalborg University Hospital.

Funding for the study was provided by Van Andel Institute through the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer® Epigenetics Dream Team, the Danish Cancer Society, and Greater Copenhagen Health Science Partners.

articles.personality_title: Daily vitamin C may improve survival in early blood cancer patients, trial finds
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – People with certain early blood disorders and cancers often have low vitamin C levels. Scientists wanted to see if taking vitamin C could help these patients live longer and stay healthier.

**What happened** – A clinical trial called EVITA tested giving 1,000 mg of vitamin C daily for a year to 109 patients with precancerous blood conditions or early-stage blood cancers. Half took vitamin C, and half took a placebo. The study was done at hospitals in Denmark and the US and was carefully designed so neither patients nor doctors knew who got the vitamin until the end.

**Impact** – Patients who took vitamin C had fewer health problems and were more likely to be alive after about three years than those who did not. Vitamin C also changed immune signals in the body that may help slow the growth of abnormal blood cells. This is important because there are currently no approved treatments to stop these early blood conditions from turning into serious leukemia.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to do a larger phase 3 trial to confirm these results. They also plan to study how vitamin C affects blood cells and gene activity to better understand how it might prevent cancer from developing.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Taking vitamin C daily shows promise as a simple way to improve survival and reduce complications in people with early blood disorders that can lead to leukemia.

articles.personality_title_es: La vitamina C diaria podría mejorar la supervivencia en pacientes con cáncer de sangre temprano, según un ensayo

articles.title: Parasite-infected mosquitoes released in Europe for first time
articles.summary: Male mosquitoes infected with a parasite have been released in Barcelona to reduce the number of insects that can transmit infections such as dengue
articles.content:
Male mosquitoes infected with a parasite have been released in Barcelona to reduce the number of insects that can transmit infections such as dengue

The Asian tiger mosquito is established in many European countries Bryan Reynolds / Alamy

More than half a million male mosquitoes carrying a parasite called wolbachia have been released in Barcelona. When these mate with females, the eggs won’t hatch, reducing the number of mosquitoes in the city and the risk of people getting mosquito-borne infections, such as dengue.

The approach is already being used in Singapore, but this is the first large-scale release in Europe. “In Barcelona, we are talking about the first example of a real introduction in the public spaces of the city,” says Rubén Bueno Mari at pest-control company Rentokil.

Globally, mosquito-borne infections are a growing problem because of the spread of invasive species, aided by global warming. In Europe, the main concern is the Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus), a daytime-feeding insect with stripy legs that has evolved to thrive in human environments.

Advertisement

The species, which can spread diseases such as dengue and chikungunya, is now established in 16 countries in Europe, including Spain, leading to record numbers of cases of these conditions. In August, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control warned that more needs to be done to tackle mosquito-borne infections.

The Asian tiger mosquito can breed in very small amounts of water, such as rainwater-filled pieces of rubbish. This means conventional methods, such as putting insecticides in large pools of water, don’t work well, says Bueno Mari. Now, in conjunction with a Google project called Debug, Rentokil is deploying a variant of the sterile insect technique.

This takes advantage of the fact that many female insects mate only once, so if they mate with a sterile male, their eggs won’t hatch. In the 1950s and 60s, this approach eliminated screwworm from the US and Mexico.

But sterile males are produced by zapping them with radiation, which means they don’t live long and makes them less likely to mate. To get around this, Debug is instead taking advantage of an extraordinary bacterial parasite called wolbachia that infects many insects. Wolbachia is passed down in eggs, and one of its many tricks is preventing infected males from fertilising female eggs that are uninfected or carry a different strain of the parasite.

In other words, wolbachia-infected male mosquitoes are effectively sterile. This approach is known as the incompatible insect technique. In very small earlier trials in Rome, the release of wolbachia-infected males reduced the number of viable eggs by nearly 90 per cent, according to Rentokil and Debug.

In Barcelona, releases began in mid-August after regulators gave the go-ahead, says Bueno Mari. Each week, 80,000 males are produced at Debug’s breeding facility in Miami, Florida, and flown to Spain. The releases, which are being funded by Rentokil and Debug, will cease in mid-November and continue from May.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

One issue with this approach is that it requires highly accurate separating of male and female mosquitoes to prevent the release of fertile females and the potential spread of wolbachia locally, which would render the strategy ineffective. Debug is using an automated process based on AI image recognition to do this, but Bueno Mari couldn’t say what percentage of females get released. “This is part of the information that we would like to extract, thanks to these trials,” he says.

However, the mosquitoes being bred and released are the same strain of the insect that is already present in Spain, he says. This means that, even if some females survive and breed, there is no chance of introducing other strains.

Even if the parasite did proliferate, wolbachia-infected mosquitoes are less likely to spread infections – in fact, the parasite is being deliberately introduced to mosquitoes in some places as an alternative strategy for reducing the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. What’s more, using a different strain of wolbachia can restore the effectiveness of the incompatible male technique.

In Singapore, wolbachia-infected male Aedes aegypti mosquitoes have been released in some parts of the city, but not in others, to assess the method’s effectiveness. A study published earlier this year concluded that the technique reduced dengue cases by 70 per cent. Some people living in treated areas may have been infected when in non-treated areas, so protection might be even higher if entire cities are treated.

“There is no single magic solution to stop the spread of mosquitoes and mosquito-borne diseases,” says Bueno Mari. “We are always talking about integrated mosquito management, but this is a new solution that can help us in a different way, so it’s promising.”

Debug is seeking permission for releases in Florida and California. Others groups are developing so-called gene drives that would spread among mosquitoes and either wipe them out or block the spread of infections.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the first large-scale release in Europe of male mosquitoes infected with the wolbachia parasite to reduce populations of disease-carrying mosquitoes, thereby lowering the risk of mosquito-borne infections like dengue. This represents a significant, innovative public health intervention with broad impact potential for many people in affected regions. The article provides detailed context on the method, its prior success in other countries, and the challenges involved, demonstrating substance and significance.
articles.personality_title: Barcelona releases parasite-infected mosquitoes to fight dengue
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Mosquitoes can carry diseases like dengue and chikungunya, which are spreading in Europe because of a type called the Asian tiger mosquito. This mosquito lives near people and can breed in tiny amounts of water, making it hard to control with usual methods like insecticides.

**What happened** – For the first time in Europe, Barcelona released over half a million male mosquitoes infected with a parasite called wolbachia. These males mate with female mosquitoes, but the eggs don’t hatch, so fewer mosquitoes grow up. The releases started in August 2023 and will continue until November, then start again in May. The mosquitoes are bred in Miami and flown to Barcelona.

**Impact** – This method, called the incompatible insect technique, was tried before in places like Singapore and Rome with good results. In Singapore, it helped reduce dengue cases by 70%. Unlike older methods, this one uses a natural parasite to make male mosquitoes unable to produce baby mosquitoes. This is important because it can lower disease risk without using harmful chemicals.

**What’s next step** – Scientists will keep testing to see how well the method works in Barcelona and improve it. They will check how many females accidentally get released, since only males should be released. Other places like Florida and California are asking permission to try this too. Researchers are also working on new ideas like gene drives to control mosquitoes in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Barcelona’s release of wolbachia-infected male mosquitoes offers a new way to reduce disease-carrying mosquitoes and protect people from infections like dengue.
articles.personality_title_fr: Barcelone libère des moustiques infectés par un parasite pour lutter contre la dengue
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les moustiques peuvent transmettre des maladies comme la dengue et la chikungunya, qui se propagent en Europe à cause d’un moustique appelé tigre asiatique. Ce moustique vit près des humains et peut se reproduire dans de très petites quantités d’eau, ce qui rend son contrôle difficile avec les méthodes habituelles comme les insecticides.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Pour la première fois en Europe, Barcelone a libéré plus d’un demi-million de moustiques mâles infectés par un parasite nommé wolbachia. Ces mâles s’accouplent avec les femelles, mais les œufs ne peuvent pas éclore, donc moins de moustiques grandissent. Les lâchers ont commencé en août 2023 et continueront jusqu’en novembre, puis reprendront en mai. Les moustiques sont élevés à Miami puis envoyés à Barcelone.

**Impact** – Cette méthode, appelée technique des insectes incompatibles, a déjà été testée à Singapour et à Rome avec de bons résultats. À Singapour, elle a permis de réduire les cas de dengue de 70 %. Contrairement aux méthodes anciennes, celle-ci utilise un parasite naturel pour rendre les moustiques mâles incapables de produire des bébés moustiques. C’est important car cela baisse le risque de maladie sans utiliser de produits chimiques nocifs.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques continueront d’évaluer l’efficacité de la méthode à Barcelone et chercheront à l’améliorer. Ils vérifieront combien de femelles sont accidentellement libérées, car seules les mâles doivent être relâchés. D’autres endroits comme la Floride et la Californie demandent aussi la permission d’essayer cette technique. Les chercheurs développent aussi de nouvelles idées comme les « gene drives » pour contrôler les moustiques à l’avenir.

**Une phrase clé** – La libération de moustiques mâles infectés par la wolbachia à Barcelone offre une nouvelle méthode pour réduire les moustiques porteurs de maladies et protéger les gens contre la dengue.
articles.personality_title_es: Barcelona libera mosquitos infectados con parásitos para combatir el dengue
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los mosquitos pueden transmitir enfermedades como el dengue y el chikungunya, que están aumentando en Europa debido a un mosquito llamado tigre asiático. Este mosquito vive cerca de las personas y puede reproducirse en pequeñas cantidades de agua, lo que dificulta controlarlo con métodos tradicionales como insecticidas.

**Qué pasó** – Por primera vez en Europa, Barcelona liberó más de medio millón de mosquitos machos infectados con un parásito llamado wolbachia. Estos machos se aparean con hembras, pero los huevos no eclosionan, por lo que nacen menos mosquitos. Las liberaciones comenzaron en agosto de 2023 y continuarán hasta noviembre, luego se reanudarán en mayo. Los mosquitos se crían en Miami y se envían a Barcelona.

**Impacto** – Este método, llamado técnica de insectos incompatibles, ya se ha probado en Singapur y Roma con buenos resultados. En Singapur ayudó a reducir los casos de dengue en un 70%. En lugar de usar insecticidas, usa un parásito natural para hacer que los mosquitos machos no puedan producir descendencia. Esto es importante porque reduce el riesgo de enfermedades sin usar químicos dañinos.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán evaluando qué tan bien funciona el método en Barcelona y buscarán mejorarlo. Verificarán cuántas hembras se liberan por error, ya que solo deben liberar machos. Otros lugares como Florida y California también están pidiendo permiso para probarlo. Además, los investigadores trabajan en nuevas ideas como los «gene drives» para controlar mosquitos en el futuro.

**Una frase clave** – La liberación de mosquitos machos infectados con wolbachia en Barcelona es una nueva forma de reducir los mosquitos que transmiten enfermedades y proteger a las personas del dengue.
